pages.title: Programming
pages.desc: The hub of this wiki: writing instructions a machine can execute, and everything that makes that hard: languages, paradigms, data structures, the systems underneath, the tools around, and the people who figured it out first.

pages.title: Python
pages.desc: A dynamically typed, garbage-collected language created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991; indentation-delimited blocks, batteries-included standard library, and the reference implementation CPython.

pages.title: CPython and the GIL
pages.desc: CPython is the reference interpreter. Its Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, which is why CPU-bound threading did not scale, and why PEP 703 introduced an optional free-threaded build.

pages.title: Type hints
pages.desc: Optional static type annotations added by PEP 484 in Python 3.5 (2015); ignored at runtime, checked by external tools such as mypy and pyright.

pages.title: JavaScript
pages.desc: The language of the web, created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995 and standardised as ECMAScript; single-threaded with an event loop, prototype-based objects, and since ES2015 a steady yearly release cadence.

pages.title: TypeScript
pages.desc: A statically typed superset of JavaScript from Microsoft, first released in 2012 and led by Anders Hejlsberg; it compiles to plain JavaScript and uses structural typing.

pages.title: Node.js
pages.desc: A server-side JavaScript runtime created by Ryan Dahl in 2009 on top of the V8 engine, built around non-blocking I/O and the npm package ecosystem.

pages.title: Event loop
pages.desc: The scheduling model behind JavaScript's single thread: a call stack, task queues, and a loop that runs the next task when the stack is empty.

pages.title: Rust
pages.desc: A systems language started by Graydon Hoare at Mozilla, 1.0 in 2015; memory safety without a garbage collector through ownership and borrowing, enforced at compile time.

pages.title: Ownership and borrowing
pages.desc: Each value has exactly one owner; references borrow it either shared (many readers) or mutable (one writer), never both at once, and the borrow checker proves lifetimes line up.

pages.title: Cargo and crates
pages.desc: Rust's build tool and package manager; crates are published to crates.io, versions follow semver, and Cargo.lock pins the exact dependency graph.

pages.title: Go
pages.desc: Designed at Google by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson, announced in 2009, 1.0 in 2012; garbage collected, statically typed, with goroutines and channels for concurrency and gofmt ending formatting debates.

pages.title: Goroutines and channels
pages.desc: Lightweight threads multiplexed onto OS threads by the Go runtime, communicating through typed channels; the motto is "do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating".

pages.title: C
pages.desc: Dennis Ritchie's language from Bell Labs (1972), in which Unix was rewritten in 1973; manual memory management, pointers, and a standard (C89 through C23) that leaves much behaviour undefined on purpose.

pages.title: Pointers and memory
pages.desc: A pointer is a variable holding an address. Pointer arithmetic, null, dangling pointers and buffer overruns are where C's power and its security record both come from.

pages.title: Undefined behaviour
pages.desc: Operations the C standard deliberately leaves unspecified (signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, data races). Compilers may assume they never happen, which enables optimisation and produces surprising code.

pages.title: Haskell
pages.desc: A purely functional, lazily evaluated language defined by committee in 1990; type classes, Hindley–Milner-style inference, and monads to sequence effects. GHC is the dominant compiler.

pages.title: Lisp and Scheme
pages.desc: John McCarthy's Lisp (1958) introduced symbolic expressions, code as data, and garbage collection; Scheme (1975) distilled it with lexical scope and tail calls, and Clojure (2007) brought it to the JVM.

pages.title: SQL
pages.desc: The declarative query language for relational databases, developed at IBM in the early 1970s on Codd's relational model and standardised by ANSI in 1986.

pages.title: Functional programming
pages.desc: Programs as compositions of functions: first-class functions, immutability and pure functions, rooted in Alonzo Church's lambda calculus of the 1930s.

pages.title: Immutability
pages.desc: Values that never change after creation; updates produce new values. Removes whole classes of bugs and makes sharing across threads safe.

pages.title: Higher-order functions
pages.desc: Functions that take or return functions: map, filter, reduce, compose, and the decorators and middleware built from them.

pages.title: Object-oriented programming
pages.desc: Bundling state with the operations on it: objects, classes or prototypes, encapsulation and polymorphism. Simula 67 introduced classes; Alan Kay's Smalltalk coined the term.

pages.title: SOLID principles
pages.desc: Five design principles popularised by Robert C. Martin: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion.

pages.title: Composition over inheritance
pages.desc: Prefer building behaviour from small components to deep class hierarchies; a core recommendation of the 1994 Design Patterns book.

pages.title: Type systems
pages.desc: Rules that assign types to expressions and reject programs that misuse them. Static vs dynamic, strong vs weak, nominal vs structural, with inference to reduce annotations.

pages.title: Generics
pages.desc: Parametric polymorphism: writing code once for any type that satisfies a constraint. ML had it in the 1970s; Java added it in 2004, Go in 2022.

pages.title: Algebraic data types
pages.desc: Product types (structs, tuples) and sum types (enums with payloads, tagged unions). Pattern matching over them makes impossible states unrepresentable.

pages.title: Type inference
pages.desc: Letting the compiler deduce types from usage. Hindley–Milner (1969/1978) gives ML and Haskell full inference; Rust, TypeScript and Go infer locally.

pages.title: Concurrency
pages.desc: Structuring programs as independently progressing parts: threads, async tasks, actors, channels, and the locks and races in between.

pages.title: Async/await
pages.desc: Syntax that lets non-blocking code read like blocking code; popularised by C# 5.0 in 2012 and now in Python, JavaScript, Rust, Swift and Kotlin.

pages.title: Actors and message passing
pages.desc: Carl Hewitt's actor model (1973): isolated units with private state that communicate only by messages. Erlang built an industry on it; Akka and Orleans brought it to the JVM and .NET.

pages.title: Locks and data races
pages.desc: A data race is two threads accessing the same memory, at least one writing, with no synchronisation. Mutexes prevent it; deadlocks are what you get for using them badly.

pages.title: Big-O notation
pages.desc: Describing how running time or memory grows with input size, ignoring constants: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²). The vocabulary for comparing algorithms.

pages.title: Hash tables
pages.desc: Key-value storage with O(1) average lookup: hash the key to a bucket, resolve collisions by chaining or open addressing, resize when the load factor grows.

pages.title: Trees
pages.desc: Hierarchical structures of nodes and children. Binary search trees give ordered lookup, B-trees power databases and filesystems, tries index strings by prefix.

pages.title: Binary search trees
pages.desc: Each node's left subtree holds smaller keys and right subtree larger ones; search, insert and delete are O(height), which is O(log n) when balanced.

pages.title: B-trees
pages.desc: Wide, shallow balanced trees (Bayer and McCreight, 1972) designed for storage that reads in blocks; the index structure in most databases and many filesystems.

pages.title: Tries
pages.desc: Prefix trees where each edge is a character; lookup is O(key length) regardless of how many keys are stored, which is why autocomplete and routers use them.

pages.title: Graphs
pages.desc: Nodes connected by edges, directed or not, weighted or not. Traversal, shortest paths and ordering problems; the structure under maps, dependency resolution and this very visualisation.

pages.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
pages.desc: Shortest paths from one source in a graph with non-negative edge weights; conceived by Edsger Dijkstra in 1956 and published in 1959, O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap.

pages.title: Topological sort
pages.desc: An ordering of a directed acyclic graph in which every edge points forward; the algorithm behind build systems, package installs and spreadsheet recalculation.

pages.title: Sorting
pages.desc: Putting things in order; comparison sorts cannot beat Ω(n log n), and the interesting differences are stability, memory and behaviour on real data.

pages.title: Quicksort
pages.desc: Tony Hoare's 1959 divide-and-conquer sort: pick a pivot, partition, recurse. O(n log n) on average, O(n²) worst case, in place and cache-friendly.

pages.title: Mergesort
pages.desc: Split, sort each half, merge; described by John von Neumann in 1945. Guaranteed O(n log n), stable, needs O(n) extra space.

pages.title: Timsort
pages.desc: Tim Peters' hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort (2002), built for Python; it finds runs that are already ordered and merges them, so nearly sorted data sorts in near-linear time.

pages.title: Dynamic programming
pages.desc: Solving problems with overlapping subproblems by storing answers: memoisation top-down or tabulation bottom-up. Richard Bellman named it in the 1950s.

pages.title: Recursion
pages.desc: A function defined in terms of itself, with a base case to stop. Natural for trees and divide-and-conquer; limited by stack depth unless the language eliminates tail calls.

pages.title: Memory management
pages.desc: Where values live and when they are freed: stack frames and heap allocations, manual free, reference counting, tracing garbage collection, or ownership checked at compile time.

pages.title: Stack vs heap
pages.desc: The stack holds fixed-size frames for active calls and frees them on return; the heap holds dynamically sized or long-lived data and must be managed.

pages.title: Garbage collection
pages.desc: Automatically reclaiming unreachable memory, invented by McCarthy for Lisp in 1959; mark-and-sweep, copying and generational collectors trade pause time against throughput.

pages.title: Reference counting
pages.desc: Each object tracks how many references point at it and is freed at zero; deterministic and simple, but cycles leak without a backup collector and the counts cost on every copy.

pages.title: Compilers and interpreters
pages.desc: Turning source text into something that runs: lexing, parsing, semantic analysis, intermediate representation, optimisation and code generation, or interpreting an IR directly, or JIT-compiling it at runtime.

pages.title: Lexing and parsing
pages.desc: Lexers turn characters into tokens; parsers turn tokens into a syntax tree according to a grammar, by recursive descent, LR tables or Pratt-style precedence climbing.

pages.title: LLVM
pages.desc: A compiler infrastructure started by Chris Lattner at the University of Illinois in 2000 (released 2003): a typed IR plus optimisers and back ends shared by Clang, Rust, Swift and many more.

pages.title: JIT compilation
pages.desc: Compiling at runtime using observed behaviour: V8, the JVM's HotSpot and PyPy start interpreting, profile hot code and compile it with speculative optimisations that deoptimise when assumptions break.

pages.title: Operating systems
pages.desc: The layer that shares a machine between programs: processes and threads, virtual memory, files, system calls and scheduling. Unix (1969) and its descendants define the vocabulary.

pages.title: Processes and threads
pages.desc: A process is an address space plus resources; threads share that address space and are scheduled independently. Isolation versus cheap communication.

pages.title: Virtual memory
pages.desc: Each process sees its own flat address space; the MMU and page tables map pages to physical frames, swap, or nothing at all, and a page fault is how the kernel finds out.

pages.title: Networking
pages.desc: How programs talk across machines: the TCP/IP stack, sockets, HTTP and TLS, and the latency and failure modes that distributed systems inherit.

pages.title: TCP/IP
pages.desc: IP routes packets between hosts; TCP (Cerf and Kahn, 1974) turns them into a reliable ordered byte stream with a three-way handshake, retransmission and congestion control; UDP skips all of that.

pages.title: HTTP
pages.desc: The web's request/response protocol: HTTP/1.1 (1997) text over TCP, HTTP/2 (2015) multiplexed binary frames, HTTP/3 (2022) over QUIC on UDP; TLS underneath for https.

pages.title: Databases
pages.desc: Durable, queryable, concurrent storage: the relational model and SQL, indexes built on B-trees, transactions with ACID guarantees, and the normal forms that keep data consistent.

pages.title: Indexes
pages.desc: Auxiliary structures, usually B-trees, that turn full-table scans into logarithmic lookups at the cost of extra writes and storage; the query planner decides when to use them.

pages.title: Transactions and ACID
pages.desc: Atomic, consistent, isolated, durable: a group of operations that either all happen or none do, even if the power fails halfway. Härder and Reuter coined ACID in 1983.

pages.title: Normalisation
pages.desc: Organising tables so each fact is stored once: first, second and third normal form remove repeating groups and partial or transitive dependencies; denormalisation trades that back for read speed.

pages.title: Unicode and text encoding
pages.desc: Unicode assigns code points to characters; UTF-8 (Thompson and Pike, 1992) encodes them in one to four bytes while staying ASCII-compatible, which is why it won the web.

pages.title: Floating point
pages.desc: IEEE 754 (1985) binary floating point: a sign, exponent and 53-bit significand for doubles. Most decimals are not representable, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3.

pages.title: Git
pages.desc: Linus Torvalds' distributed version control system from 2005: a content-addressed store of snapshots where branches are just pointers to commits.

pages.title: Branching and merging
pages.desc: Diverge to work in isolation, then merge: three-way merges find the common ancestor, conflicts are where both sides changed the same lines.

pages.title: Rebasing
pages.desc: Replaying commits onto a new base to produce a linear history; rewrites commit hashes, so never rebase commits others have already pulled.

pages.title: Testing
pages.desc: Checking software does what it should, automatically and repeatedly: unit tests for pieces, integration tests for seams, property-based tests for laws, fuzzing for the inputs nobody imagined.

pages.title: Unit tests
pages.desc: Small tests of one unit in isolation. The xUnit family descends from Kent Beck's SUnit for Smalltalk; JUnit (1997) made it universal.

pages.title: Property-based testing
pages.desc: State a law (reversing twice is identity; decode(encode(x)) == x) and let the framework generate hundreds of inputs and shrink failures. QuickCheck (Claessen and Hughes, 2000) started it.

pages.title: Fuzzing
pages.desc: Feeding programs random or mutated inputs to find crashes; Barton Miller coined the term in 1988, AFL (2013) made coverage-guided fuzzing mainstream, and OSS-Fuzz runs it continuously for open source.

pages.title: Debugging
pages.desc: Finding out why the program does what it does instead of what you meant: reproduce, bisect, inspect, fix, and add the test that would have caught it.

pages.title: Code review
pages.desc: A second pair of eyes before code lands: catches bugs, spreads knowledge and keeps style consistent. Works best on small changes with automated checks handling the mechanical parts.

pages.title: CI/CD
pages.desc: Continuous integration runs the build and tests on every push; continuous delivery keeps the main branch deployable and automates releases.

pages.title: Package managers
pages.desc: Fetching, versioning and resolving dependencies: npm, pip, Cargo, Go modules. Semantic versioning, lockfiles and the supply-chain risk of trusting a thousand strangers.

pages.title: Shell and the Unix philosophy
pages.desc: Small programs that do one thing well, composed with pipes over text streams. Doug McIlroy's pipes (1973) and philosophy are why the command line is still the universal glue.

pages.title: Regular expressions
pages.desc: Patterns for matching text, from Kleene's regular languages (1951) through Thompson's construction (1968) to today's backtracking engines and their catastrophic cases.

pages.title: Documentation
pages.desc: Writing for the next reader, including yourself: READMEs, docstrings, reference docs and the four kinds of documentation (tutorial, how-to, reference, explanation) that Diátaxis separates.

pages.title: Ada Lovelace
pages.desc: 1815–1852. Her 1843 notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine include an algorithm for Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program, and the insight that such a machine could manipulate symbols, not only numbers.

pages.title: Alan Turing
pages.desc: 1912–1954. His 1936 paper defined the abstract machine that bears his name and proved the halting problem undecidable; later he led codebreaking at Bletchley Park and proposed the imitation game.

pages.title: Grace Hopper
pages.desc: 1906–1992. US Navy rear admiral and computer scientist; wrote the A-0 system (1952), one of the first compilers, led FLOW-MATIC, and shaped COBOL's English-like syntax.

pages.title: Edsger Dijkstra
pages.desc: 1930–2002. Dutch computer scientist: shortest-path algorithm, semaphores, structured programming, "Go To Statement Considered Harmful" (1968), Turing Award 1972.

pages.title: Donald Knuth
pages.desc: Born 1938. Author of The Art of Computer Programming (from 1968), creator of TeX (1978) and literate programming, Turing Award 1974, and source of the line about premature optimisation.

pages.title: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie
pages.desc: Bell Labs colleagues who built Unix (1969) and C (1972), shared the 1983 Turing Award; Thompson went on to UTF-8 (1992) and Go (2009), Ritchie co-wrote the C book (1978).

pages.title: Barbara Liskov
pages.desc: Born 1939. Designed CLU (1970s), which introduced abstract data types and iterators; stated the substitution principle (1987); Turing Award 2008.

pages.title: John McCarthy
pages.desc: 1927–2011. Invented Lisp (1958), garbage collection (1959) and the term "artificial intelligence" (1955); Turing Award 1971.

pages.title: Margaret Hamilton
pages.desc: Born 1936. Led the team that wrote the Apollo Guidance Computer flight software at MIT; her priority-scheduling and error-recovery design let Apollo 11 land despite overloaded alarms. Popularised the term "software engineering".

pages.title: Linus Torvalds
pages.desc: Born 1969. Released Linux in 1991 as a hobby kernel that now runs most of the internet, and wrote Git in 2005 when the kernel needed a new version-control system.

pages.title: Guido van Rossum
pages.desc: Born 1956. Created Python in 1989–1991 at CWI and led it as "Benevolent Dictator For Life" until stepping down in 2018 after the PEP 572 debate.

pages.title: Brendan Eich
pages.desc: Born 1961. Created JavaScript at Netscape in 1995 in about ten days, co-founded Mozilla, and later founded Brave.
